To implement birth notification, the MOHW established the 'Birth Notification Operation Plan' and, after multiple negotiations with the Ministry of the Interior (competent authority for the Child Welfare Act), the MOI finalized and announced the 'Birth Notification Workflow' on 13 September 1994. That December 28 the MOHW promulgated the newly revised 'Birth Certificate' and 'Stillbirth Certificate', and paper-based birth notification began in March 1995. 2. From 2004, medical units switched to online reporting and stopped using paper, while household-registration reporting still used both methods; after continued coordination between the HPA and the MOI's Department of Household Registration, online birth notification was fully implemented from 2005, entirely eliminating paper mailing. 3. On 28 May 2003 the Child Welfare Act and Youth Welfare Act were merged and revised into the Child and Youth Welfare Act, Article 13 of which requires: 'Within 7 days of a fetus's birth, the attendant shall report the birth data to the household-registration and health authorities.' 4. On 30 November 2011 the Child and Youth Welfare and Rights Protection Act was amended, Article 14 requiring: 'Within 7 days of birth, the attendant shall report the birth data to the health authority; the same applies for stillbirths.' For births outside a hospital, clinic, or midwifery clinic where a birth certificate cannot be obtained, a DNA parentage report from a medical institution or a birth-notification form issued by a licensed medical professional must be presented for birth registration. 5. Unlike 'birth registration', 'birth notification' covers all births in Taiwan (regardless of nationality): a. live newborns; b. stillbirths of >=20 weeks' gestation or >=500 g. (Quoted from the HPA's birth-notification background notes.)

Enrollment/disenrollment types: (1) Enroll: joins NHI upon meeting eligibility. (2) Disenroll: 1) death; 2) serving a sentence in prison/detention, or a security/reformatory measure, for 2+ months; 3) missing for 6 months (or from the disaster date if missing due to disaster); 4) becoming an active-duty officer, NCO, soldier, or military-academy funded student (changed to 'transfer out' on 2001-02-01); 5) loss of enrollment conditions (e.g. household moved out, residence permit expired, foreigner's work/study ended and left). (3) Transfer in: 1) change of insurer unit; 2) change of insured identity. (4) Transfer out: 1) change of insurer unit; 2) change of insured identity. (5) Cancel: NHIA cancels a doubly-enrolled insured person. (6) Interrupted transfer in: everyone eligible must enroll; if after enrolling a gap in enrollment arose (job change, identity change, address move, etc.) with unpaid premiums, and the person re-enters NHI. (7) Interrupted transfer out: similarly, a gap leading to exit from NHI. (8) Resume: 1) a missing person found within 6 months should cancel suspension and pay back premiums; if not found after 6 months, insurance is terminated retroactively from the suspension month and disenrollment processed; 2) a person abroad 6+ months resumes on the return date, but one abroad under 6 months cancels suspension and pays back premiums. (9) Suspend: 1) registered missing but under 6 months; 2) continuously detained 2+ months; 3) planned to be abroad 6+ months, except deep-sea fishing-vessel crew; 4) continued-coverage dependents (children, grandchildren) aged 20+ without earning capacity (e.g. disability-certificate holders) or still studying without employment. (10) Suspend-resume: the field changes to 'suspend-resume' when resuming after suspension.

1. To implement birth-notification work, the Ministry of Health and Welfare established the "Birth Notification Operations Plan" and held repeated consultations with the Ministry of the Interior, the competent authority for the Child Welfare Act. The Ministry of the Interior finalized and announced the "Birth Notification Operating Procedure" on September 13, 1994 (ROC year 83). On December 28 of the same year, the Ministry of Health and Welfare announced the newly revised "Birth Certificate" and "Stillbirth Certificate," and paper-based birth notification began in March 1995 (ROC year 84).
2. Starting in 2004 (ROC year 93), medical institutions switched to online notification and stopped using paper forms, while household-registration offices continued to use both notification methods in parallel. Following continued coordination between the Health Promotion Administration and the Ministry of the Interior's Department of Household Registration Affairs, online birth notification was fully implemented starting in 2005 (ROC year 94), completely eliminating the mailing of paper forms.
3. On May 28, 2003 (ROC year 92), the "Child Welfare Act" and the "Youth Welfare Act" were merged and amended into the "Child and Youth Welfare Act," Article 13 of which provides: "Within 7 days of a fetus's birth, the person who assisted the delivery shall report the relevant birth information to the household registration and health authorities for the record."
4. On November 30, 2011 (ROC year 100), the "Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act" was amended and promulgated; Article 14 provides: "Within 7 days of a fetus's birth, the person who assisted the delivery shall report the relevant birth information to the health authority for the record; the same applies in the case of a stillbirth." In addition, for births that did not occur in a hospital, clinic, or midwifery institution and for which a birth certificate cannot be obtained, birth registration may be completed by presenting either a DNA parentage test report issued by a medical institution or a birth notification form issued by a licensed medical or nursing professional.
5. Unlike "birth registration," "birth notification" covers all of the following born in Taiwan (regardless of nationality):
a. live-born newborns;
b. stillbirths at ≥20 weeks of gestation or with a birth weight of ≥500 grams.
(Quoted from the Health Promotion Administration's background description of birth notification)

2. Starting with diagnosis year 2002, the long-form TCDB first collected data on cervical cancer, breast cancer, oral cancer, colorectal cancer, liver cancer, and lung cancer.
3. Starting with diagnosis year 2008, prostate cancer, gastric cancer, esophageal cancer, and bladder cancer were added, bringing the total to ten major cancers.
4. Starting with diagnosis year 2009, nasopharyngeal cancer, major salivary gland cancer, corpus uteri cancer, ovarian cancer, and hematologic malignancies were added, bringing the total to fifteen major cancers.
5. Starting with diagnosis year 2013, laryngeal cancer was added, bringing the total to sixteen major cancers.
6. Starting with diagnosis year 2022, pancreatic cancer was added, bringing the total to seventeen major cancers.
7. Three versions of AJCC cancer staging are used within the long-form database:
Cases diagnosed with cancer between 2003 and 2009 are staged according to AJCC 6th edition.
Cases diagnosed with cancer between 2010 and 2017 are staged according to AJCC 7th edition.
Cases diagnosed with cancer from 2018 onward are staged according to AJCC 8th edition.
Cervical cancer cases diagnosed from 2021 onward are staged according to AJCC 9th edition.
Starting from AJCC 9th edition, stage information is updated for each cancer type as needed.
8. For guidance on analyzing long-form data, refer to the Taiwan Cancer Registry Center website: https://twcr.tw/?p=3284.
9. To analyze detailed information such as radiotherapy equipment or dose, be sure to consult the Taiwan Cancer Registry Long Form Abstracting Manual and pay attention to the relationships among the various radiotherapy fields.

1. Starting in 2007, cancer registry long-form reporting has used the 95-field format, which applies to all cases diagnosed between 2002 and 2010; therefore the 95-field cancer registry long-form database includes some cases diagnosed between 2002 and 2006.
2. In addition to the cervical, breast, colorectal, oral, lung, and liver cancers reported in 2007, and the prostate, gastric, esophageal, and bladder cancers added in 2008, long-form hospitals were required to report nasopharyngeal cancer, major salivary gland cancer, corpus uteri cancer, ovarian cancer, and hematologic malignancies starting in 2009, for a total of 15 cancer types.
3. Because the combination of TNM and Stage differs between AJCC 6th and 7th edition staging for some cancer types, care should be taken when interpreting stage distributions across different diagnosis years.
4. First-recurrence data records whether a case experienced its first cancer recurrence within five years of follow-up after the cancer diagnosis; only cases classified as 1 or 2 are required to have this field tracked and reported. If, after a first recurrence within five years, further recurrences occur, this field records only the first recurrence status; if the first recurrence occurs more than five years after diagnosis, this field is recorded as no recurrence. Recurrence information is reported only twice: once at one year and once at five years after diagnosis.
5. Because hospital reporting of cancer registry data is time-constrained, the date-of-death and cause-of-death fields are relatively incomplete; if complete data is needed, it is recommended to apply for the Cause of Death Statistics File instead.
6. This user manual is based on the Taiwan Cancer Registry Center's manual; for details, please download from the Taiwan Cancer Registry Center website, e.g., the "2007 (ROC year 96) Taiwan Cancer Registry Abstracting Manual."

1. The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is recognized as an important method for monitoring the current status and trends of national health. In Taiwan, the NHIS, conducted once every four years, has completed three rounds of surveys in 2001, 2005, and 2009. In 2001, in view of the increasingly serious trend of illegal drug and substance abuse both domestically and internationally, and considering its adverse health effects, questions on drugs and other addictive substances were added for the first time in 2005, expanding the survey into the "National Health Interview and Drug Abuse Survey." Also starting in 2005, the sampling unit changed from the household to the individual, and the 2009 survey largely followed the 2005 model.
2. This survey mainly continues the framework of the 2009 survey. Because analysis of the self-administered drug-abuse supplementary questionnaires from 2005 and 2009 found that the probability of drug-abuse behavior among completed-interview samples was only about 1.5%, the sample size was insufficient to further examine drug-abuse behavior across different age groups. Therefore, the self-administered questionnaire on the prevalence of drug abuse among the population was not included in the 2013 NHIS. The 2013 NHIS content is divided into seven major sections: personal basic information, personal health status, disease-prevention knowledge, utilization of medical and preventive-care services, personal health behavior, self-perceived health status, and work and economic status, along with supplementary modules covering "mental health (CES-D scale)," "self-perceived health status (SF-36)," "EQ-5D scale," "degree of acceptance of traditional Chinese medicine resources," and "use of traditional Chinese medicine," among others.
(Quoted from the results report of the National Health Interview and Drug Abuse Survey working team)

1. The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is recognized as an important method for monitoring the current status and trends of national health. In Taiwan, the NHIS, conducted once every four years, has completed five rounds of surveys in 2001, 2005, 2009, 2013, and 2017. In 2001, in view of the increasingly serious trend of illegal drug and substance abuse both domestically and internationally, and considering its adverse health effects, questions on drugs and other addictive substances were added for the first time in 2005, expanding the survey into the "National Health Interview and Drug Abuse Survey." Also starting in 2005, the sampling unit changed from the household to the individual; the 2009 survey first introduced "optional modules" and the "Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) system," increasing the convenience of face-to-face interviews, data-entry efficiency, and data quality.
2. The sixth NHIS was conducted from 2021 to 2022 (ROC years 110-111), expanding the survey area to include Kinmen and Lienchiang counties. This survey mainly continues the data-collection model established since 2009, using computer-assisted methods for community face-to-face interviews and self-administered questionnaires, and builds on the computer-assisted survey information system developed for the 2013 survey, with system enhancements, new features, and corrections, applied to this community health survey.
3. This survey used household registration data as the sampling frame. Based on regional population characteristics and administrative and cost considerations for survey implementation, individuals were sampled in Taiwan Area (including Penghu County), while in Kinmen and Lienchiang counties, households were used as the sampling unit, with a full census of the actual resident population of the selected address households. Interviewers used the computer-assisted personal interviewing system to conduct questionnaire surveys in each sample area. Considering differences in health issues across age groups, three types of questionnaires were designed—under 12, 12-64, and 65 and older—combining core questions with supplementary modules to increase the data items collected in each questionnaire. Fieldwork was conducted from October to December 2021 (ROC year 110) and from July to November 2022 (ROC year 111); the number of completed interviews was 24,304 in Taiwan Area, and 800 and 589 in Kinmen County and Lienchiang County, respectively.
(Quoted from the results report of the National Health Interview and Drug Abuse Survey working team)

1. Survey purpose: to collect data on the living and health conditions, childcare and parenting issues, and needs, use, and expectations regarding welfare measures of children aged 0 to under 6.
2. Survey items: child's basic information, family status, parents' status, childcare arrangements, physical condition and diet, play and recreational activities, and needs regarding child welfare policy, among others.
3. Survey area: the Taiwan-Fukien Area.
4. Survey subjects: children aged 0 to under 6 residing within the survey area.
5. Survey method: interviewers visit the respondent's residence to conduct face-to-face interviews, answered by the child's parents, adoptive parents, or primary caregiver.
6. Sampling method: stratified two-stage random sampling. The country was divided into 11 sub-populations by the six special municipalities and the northern, central, southern, eastern, and Kinmen-Matsu regions. Townships/districts within each sub-population were stratified with reference to the "2017 National Health Interview Survey Sampling Design," using cluster analysis to classify the country's 368 townships/districts into 7 types, which served as the stratification basis for sampling within each sub-population. In the first stage, townships/districts within each stratum were ordered by population size, and sample townships/districts were drawn via systematic random sampling based on cumulative township/district population. In the second stage, four strata were formed by sex and age group (0-under 3, 3-under 6); the number of samples to be completed in each stratum was allocated in proportion to that stratum's share of the region, and within each stratum, sample households were drawn via systematic random sampling after ordering by address.

Enrollment/disenrollment types: (1) Enroll: joins NHI upon meeting eligibility. (2) Disenroll: 1) death; 2) serving a sentence in prison/detention, or a security/reformatory measure, for 2+ months; 3) missing for 6 months (or from the disaster date if missing due to disaster); 4) becoming an active-duty officer, NCO, soldier, or military-academy funded student (changed to 'transfer out' on 2001-02-01); 5) loss of enrollment conditions (e.g. household moved out, residence permit expired, foreigner's work/study ended and left). (3) Transfer in: 1) change of insurer unit; 2) change of insured identity. (4) Transfer out: 1) change of insurer unit; 2) change of insured identity. (5) Cancel: NHIA cancels a doubly-enrolled insured person. (6) Interrupted transfer in: everyone eligible must enroll; if after enrolling a gap in enrollment arose (job change, identity change, address move, etc.) with unpaid premiums, and the person re-enters NHI. (7) Interrupted transfer out: similarly, a gap leading to exit from NHI. (8) Resume: 1) a missing person found within 6 months should cancel suspension and pay back premiums; if not found after 6 months, insurance is terminated retroactively from the suspension month and disenrollment processed; 2) a person abroad 6+ months resumes on the return date, but one abroad under 6 months cancels suspension and pays back premiums. 1. This survey was conducted pursuant to Article 10 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act, mainly to collect data on the living conditions of Taiwan's population aged 55 and older. This survey focused on family caregivers, and additionally surveyed care-related questions for the primary family caregivers of persons aged 65 and older who are unable to live independently.
2. The questionnaire is divided into three types: "65 and older," "55-64," and "primary family caregiver." The content covers: family and living conditions, health status, daily living and self-care ability (65 and older only), employment status, social activity status, family caregiving conditions, economic status, understanding of elderly welfare measures, willingness to move into elderly welfare institutions, elderly apartments, elderly housing, community care centers, or nursing homes, living conditions for those already residing in such facilities, views or feelings about elderly life, and basic information, among others; the "primary family caregiver" questionnaire covers basic information, caregiving work conditions, and needs for government-provided caregiver support services.
3. This survey completed a total of 4,310 interviews for "65 and older," 2,610 for "55-64," and 469 for primary family caregivers.
4. The survey implementation plan, sampling design, and questionnaire can be found on the website of the Department of Statistics, Ministry of Health and Welfare (URL: https://dep.mohw.gov.tw/DOS/lp-1767-113.html).

e02236d972861189: 1. To implement birth notification, the MOHW established the 'Birth Notification Operation Plan' and, after multiple negotiations with the Ministry of the Interior (competent authority for the Child Welfare Act), the MOI finalized and announced the 'Birth Notification Workflow' on 13 September 1994. That December 28 the MOHW promulgated the newly revised 'Birth Certificate' and 'Stillbirth Certificate', and paper-based birth notification began in March 1995. 2. From 2004, medical units switched to online reporting and stopped using paper, while household-registration reporting still used both methods; after continued coordination between the HPA and the MOI's Department of Household Registration, online birth notification was fully implemented from 2005, entirely eliminating paper mailing. 3. On 28 May 2003 the Child Welfare Act and Youth Welfare Act were merged and revised into the Child and Youth Welfare Act, Article 13 of which requires: 'Within 7 days of a fetus's birth, the attendant shall report the birth data to the household-registration and health authorities.' 4. On 30 November 2011 the Child and Youth Welfare and Rights Protection Act was amended, Article 14 requiring: 'Within 7 days of birth, the attendant shall report the birth data to the health authority; the same applies for stillbirths.' For births outside a hospital, clinic, or midwifery clinic where a birth certificate cannot be obtained, a DNA parentage report from a medical institution or a birth-notification form issued by a licensed medical professional must be presented for birth registration. 5. Unlike 'birth registration', 'birth notification' covers all births in Taiwan (regardless of nationality): a. live newborns; b. stillbirths of >=20 weeks' gestation or >=500 g. (Quoted from the HPA's birth-notification background notes.)
